title: Covering Indexes
description: Use INCLUDE columns and index-only scans to eliminate table lookups

data.text: A covering index contains all columns required by a query, allowing the database to satisfy the query from the index alone without visiting the table. This is called an index-only scan.

data.title: Benefits
items: Reduces I/O for small result sets

data.title: Covering index for dashboard
data.content: A dashboard query needs status and total from orders for a specific customer.
data.code:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) as total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 123
GROUP BY status;

-- Covering index:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status_covering
ON orders(customer_id)
INCLUDE (status);

data.title: Tip
data.text: Use INCLUDE for non-key columns that appear only in SELECT lists. Keep filter and sort columns in the key for prefix support.

items.question: Do all databases support INCLUDE?
items.answer: PostgreSQL and SQL Server support INCLUDE. MySQL uses secondary indexes differently; all columns are already stored.

items.question: Should I make every index covering?
items.answer: No. Covering indexes are wider and more expensive to maintain. Target only frequent, performance-critical queries.

items.question: What if the table is very wide?
items.answer: Covering indexes shine on wide tables where table lookups are expensive. On narrow tables, the benefit is smaller.

data.title: Summary
data.takeaway: Covering indexes are a targeted performance optimization for known query patterns with predictable output columns.
